type_specific.meeting_summary: Arvada City Council received a study session briefing from the Infrastructure Department on parking challenges in Oldtown Arvada, including 15 years of occupancy data, preliminary results from a community survey with over 4,000 responses, and ongoing investments in the Oldtown Transit Hub and surrounding area. Staff presented three options for how to proceed with a potential paid parking program and sought council direction. Council members expressed broad support for pausing paid parking work while prioritizing improvements to the transit hub's safety, accessibility, wayfinding, and ingress/egress design.

briefings.topic: Oldtown Arvada Parking: History, Occupancy Data, Community Survey & Next Steps
briefings.presenter_name: Jacqueline Rhodess and Kelly Van Bugan
briefings.presenter_role: Director of Infrastructure (Rhodess) and Transportation Planning Manager (Van Bugan), City of Arvada Infrastructure Department
prose_paragraphs: Infrastructure Director Jacqueline Rhodess (joining remotely from Washington, D.C.) and Transportation Planning Manager Kelly Van Bugan presented a 16-slide briefing on parking demand in Oldtown Arvada, tracing the issue from 2010 to the present. On-street parking supply in the Oldtown core has shrunk from 661 spaces in 2010 to 442 today, due to the conversion of diagonal parking to parallel, the 2017 opening of the Oldtown Transit Hub (which netted only about 20 new spaces after offsetting a former RTD park-and-ride lot and the G-Line platform displacement), and the removal of roughly 50 on-street spaces when the pedestrian mall was created in 2020. Using color-coded occupancy maps from 2010, 2016, and 2025, staff showed that peak-time parking occupancy in the Oldtown core has climbed steadily, with 2025 data showing the vast majority of on-street spaces operating at 91–100% occupancy during lunch, mid-afternoon, and evening peak windows — well above the industry-standard 85th-percentile threshold at which circling behavior and illegal parking begin to emerge. By contrast, the Oldtown Transit Hub remains significantly underutilized during those same peak periods.

Staff explained that the paid parking conversation has been part of the city's official planning framework for years, appearing in both the 2023 Oldtown Strategic Reinvestment Plan and the Climate and Sustainability Action Plan, both of which underwent extensive community engagement. A 2016 parking study had already recommended exploring paid parking if time restrictions failed to resolve capacity problems; the 2025 data shows those restrictions have not resolved the issue. In response to a prior October 2024 council workshop, staff collected more granular month-by-month occupancy data from November 2024 through December 2025, confirming that evening peak occupancy averages 93% annually. Staff also described a parallel set of investments already underway: wayfinding signs added in October 2024 directing drivers to the transit hub, parking enforcement brought in-house in February 2025 with two new full-time employees, an Oldtown ambassadors program, pedestrian mall resurfacing and mural reinstallation, and roundabout design work with AURA to improve transit hub access. Two innovation concepts — a 'Southern Gateway' strategy to make the hub feel like an entry point to Oldtown, and a 'Park and Earn' rewards program to incentivize hub use — are currently in prototyping. The city has estimated approximately $350,000 in start-up costs to implement a paid parking program (including roughly $100,000 for signage and approximately $3,000 per kiosk), though some kiosk vendors offer deferred payment arrangements. Estimated annual revenue from a program was previously cited at approximately $1 million, though staff noted the exact figure depends heavily on the model chosen. Total current and planned Oldtown investment outlined in the presentation was approximately $8 million, including $2.65 million in operating budget for current operations, hub maintenance, and the ambassadors program; $378,000 in 2026 dedicated maintenance projects; and $4.92 million in Oldtown Reinvestment Plan projects.

Staff presented three options for council direction: (1) continue designing a paid parking program while fully analyzing survey results and conducting deeper community engagement before advancing; (2) pause paid parking work and prioritize hub improvements, innovation initiatives, and other Oldtown Reinvestment Plan projects first; or (3) stop paid parking design work indefinitely. A community survey closed shortly before the meeting with over 4,000 responses across three tracks (businesses/employees, visitors, and nearby residents). Staff emphasized the results are preliminary and require further analysis before being publicly reported. Key early themes included substantial skepticism across all groups, with businesses worried about customer loss, visitors questioning whether benefits justify a fee, and residents concerned about spillover parking into neighborhoods. Visitors said they would use the hub if street parking became paid; employees cited distance, safety, and lighting as barriers to using existing hub permits. Neighborhood residents reported parking is currently easy to find on their streets. Staff acknowledged that survey language avoided a direct 'for or against' question, which created some confusion, and committed to more explicit communication in future engagement rounds. Council members broadly favored a pause, with several calling for concrete hub improvements — including better ingress/egress design, improved safety and lighting, additional ADA-accessible parking, potential micro-mobility or shuttle service between the hub and the pedestrian mall, and updated wayfinding signage — before any paid parking program is advanced. Several council members also requested comparative data from other cities with free downtown parking, detailed transit hub utilization data, enforcement effectiveness metrics for the existing time-restriction zones, and a granular analysis of paid parking impacts by business type.

questions_raised: Was parking in the former free RTD lots south of Oldtown included in the 2010 parking study data, and how many people used that area?
Was the 2025 occupancy data collected using the same methodology and by the same organization as the 2010 and 2016 studies?
How many on-street ADA-accessible parking spaces were removed when the pedestrian mall road closures were implemented, and does the current supply still meet ADA compliance requirements?
Has the city analyzed whether Arvada's overall population growth accounts for increased parking demand, and was that factored into any of the studies?
Who pays for the Oldtown ambassadors program, and are other city programs being reduced to fund it?
What is the estimated cost to develop and implement a paid parking program, including kiosks, signage, and app administration fees?
Is there documented crime or safety incident data supporting residents' and employees' safety concerns about the Oldtown Transit Hub, or is it primarily perception?
Can staff provide a comparison of other cities that have maintained free downtown parking at or below the 85% occupancy threshold, and how are those programs structured?
What does 'intersection control to be determined' mean for the planned roundabout location on slide eight of the presentation?
Could a roundabout also be added on the Marshall Street side of the transit hub to eliminate the need for drivers to double back to enter?
Is the previously cited estimate of approximately $1 million in annual revenue from a paid parking program dependent on the specific program model chosen?
How long will parking in the Oldtown Transit Hub remain free, and what is the threshold in the city's intergovernmental agreement with RTD that would trigger a transition to paid hub parking?
Where exactly are the new wayfinding signs located, and can staff provide a map showing all installed sign locations?
What measures can be put in place to prevent paid on-street parking from pushing vehicles into nearby residential neighborhoods?
Can staff provide detailed utilization data from the transit hub, including self-reported purpose data from the payment kiosks and license plate camera counts?
How effectively are the existing two-hour time restrictions being enforced today, and is there a way to improve that enforcement?
What lessons can be learned from Grand Junction, Colorado's experience transitioning from free to paid downtown parking?
Can staff provide a more granular analysis of how paid parking would affect different types of Oldtown businesses, particularly high-turnover retail versus restaurants and bars?
Is there an opportunity to expand citywide use of the new in-house parking enforcement staff beyond Oldtown to address issues near schools and other locations?
Does the council's direction on paid parking contradict or conflict with the recently approved Transportation System Plan or the Climate and Sustainability Action Plan?
